report_meta.supply_chain_link: Amkor sits in the PACKAGING tier of the AI supply chain. After a foundry (e.g., TSMC) makes the silicon, the chips must be assembled into a finished package and tested — that is Amkor's job. It is the world's #2 outsourced packaging-and-test company (OSAT), and the leading non-foundry provider of advanced packaging for AI/compute, automotive, and premium smartphones. Its advanced platforms (HDFO/2.5D) are outsourced alternatives/complements to TSMC's in-house CoWoS (see reports/TSMC.json).

beginner_glossary.OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly: A company that does the BACK-END of chipmaking for others: after a foundry makes the bare silicon, the OSAT assembles it into a finished 'package' (protecting the chip and connecting it to a circuit board) and tests it. Amkor is the world's #2 OSAT (behind ASE). It owns no chip designs — it is a contract service provider, like a foundry but for packaging/test.
beginner_glossary.Packaging (semiconductor): Turning a bare silicon die into a usable chip — encasing it, wiring its connections, and (increasingly) combining multiple dies + memory into one module. 'Advanced packaging' does the complex, high-value versions needed for AI and high-performance computing.
beginner_glossary.Advanced vs mainstream packaging: Mainstream = simpler, lower-price packages (e.g., wire bond) for everyday chips. Advanced = complex, high-value packages (flip chip, fan-out, 2.5D) for AI/compute, premium phones, and advanced cars. Amkor's profit growth comes from mix-shifting toward advanced.
beginner_glossary.Wire bond / flip chip: Two ways to connect a chip to its package. Wire bond (older, cheaper) uses tiny wires; flip chip (newer) flips the chip onto bumps for faster, denser connections. Flip chip is a building block of advanced packaging.
beginner_glossary.HDFO (High-Density Fan-Out): Amkor's family of advanced packages that spread a chip's connections out over a larger area without a bulky substrate — key for AI/HPC chips. Amkor's HDFO platforms include SWIFT and S-Connect / Amkor-Connect.
beginner_glossary.SWIFT / S-Connect / Amkor-Connect: Amkor's branded advanced-packaging technologies. Management compares SWIFT to TSMC's CoWoS-R and S-Connect to TSMC's CoWoS-L — i.e., they are outsourced alternatives to the foundry's in-house AI packaging.
beginner_glossary.2.5D / silicon interposer: An advanced package where multiple chips (e.g., a processor + HBM memory) sit side-by-side on a silicon 'interposer' that wires them together at high speed. The standard way AI accelerators are built.
beginner_glossary.CoWoS (TSMC) — for comparison: TSMC's flagship in-house advanced-packaging method for AI chips. Because CoWoS capacity is scarce, customers increasingly want OUTSOURCED alternatives — which is Amkor's opportunity.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked DRAM placed next to AI processors. Amkor packages chips that integrate HBM; HBM/'advanced silicon' supply timing affects Amkor's loading.
beginner_glossary.Test: Checking that finished chips work to spec. Amkor offers test alongside packaging; it is a higher-value, sticky service.
beginner_glossary.End markets (Communications / Computing: Amkor reports revenue by where the chips go. Communications = smartphones (big Apple/iOS exposure); Computing = PCs + AI data center; Automotive & Industrial = cars (ADAS, infotainment) + industrial; Consumer = wearables, etc.
beginner_glossary.Utilization: How full Amkor's factories are running. Higher utilization spreads fixed costs over more units, lifting margins (Q1 2026 was in the low-70s%, up from the 50s a year earlier).
beginner_glossary.Operating leverage: Because factories have high fixed costs, each extra dollar of revenue at higher utilization drops a larger share to profit — why Amkor's margins jump when demand is strong.
beginner_glossary.Gross margin (OSAT context): OSAT gross margins are structurally LOW (Amkor ~14-15%) versus a foundry's (TSMC ~66%), because packaging is more labor/equipment-intensive and less differentiated than wafer-making. So Amkor's profit story is about VOLUME, utilization, and mix-shift to advanced — not high margins per unit.
beginner_glossary.EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — a cash-earnings gauge. Amkor's Q1 2026 EBITDA was $285M (16.9% margin); useful because Amkor is capital-intensive (lots of depreciation).
beginner_glossary.CapEx / capital intensity: Money spent on factories and equipment. Amkor is capital-intensive (2026 CapEx guided $2.5-3.0B on ~$7B+ revenue) because packaging needs constant new tools and buildings.
beginner_glossary.Arizona facility / CHIPS Act / ITC: Amkor's new U.S. advanced-packaging campus near TSMC's Arizona fabs. A ~$7B two-phase project, supported by a $400M U.S. CHIPS Act grant and a 35% investment tax credit (~$2.8B combined). Phase 1 completes 2027, production 2028, scaling to full impact by 2030.
beginner_glossary.Partnership / co-investment model: Amkor's customers (foundries, fabless, IDMs) increasingly help fund its capacity (prepayments, capital support) in exchange for guaranteed supply — reducing Amkor's investment risk and aligning roadmaps.
beginner_glossary.P/E ratio (Price-to-Earnings): Share price divided by yearly earnings per share. Amkor's ~48x trailing / ~38x forward P/E is HIGH for an OSAT (which historically traded ~15-20x), reflecting big AI-packaging growth expectations.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Amkor Technology is the world's #2 outsourced semiconductor assembly-and-test company (OSAT) and the leading independent (non-foundry) provider of ADVANCED packaging for AI/high-performance computing, premium smartphones, and advanced automotive chips. After a foundry makes the silicon, Amkor turns it into a finished, tested package. It is increasingly a key 'second source' for advanced AI packaging as in-house foundry capacity (e.g., TSMC's CoWoS) stays scarce.
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: Founded by James J. Kim; the Kim family retains majority control. Led by President & CEO Kevin Engel; EVP & CFO Megan Faust (both presented the Q1 2026 call).
company_snapshot.manufacturing_footprint: Global, with the most advanced packaging in Korea and Taiwan; mainstream/assembly in the Philippines, Vietnam, Japan, and China; and a new U.S. advanced-packaging campus under construction in Arizona (Phase 1 completion 2027, production 2028). A new Korea test building completes end-2026; SiP production is migrating from Korea to Vietnam to free advanced capacity. [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-27]

business_model.summary: Amkor makes money by providing outsourced packaging and test services and charging per unit, with much higher value for advanced packages than mainstream ones. Its profit lever is operating leverage: fill the factories (utilization), shift the mix toward advanced packaging, and push pricing — and margins expand. The current driver is AI: as chips get more complex and CoWoS-type capacity stays scarce, customers turn to Amkor's advanced platforms (HDFO/2.5D), and Amkor's advanced-AI-packaging revenue is guided to TRIPLE in 2026.
how_they_make_money: Advanced packaging — flip chip, HDFO (SWIFT, S-Connect), and 2.5D/silicon-interposer for AI/HPC, premium phones, and advanced auto. The high-value, fastest-growing part of the mix. [Q1 2026 call]
Mainstream packaging — wire-bond and simpler packages for everyday chips (autos' drivetrain, industrial, consumer). Lower-value but recovering (4 straight quarters of growth). [Q1 2026 call]
Test services — verifying finished chips work; a higher-value, sticky add-on to packaging.
Foundry/turnkey collaboration — outsourced work tied to foundry and IDM partners (e.g., a collaboration with Intel related to EMIB packaging). [Q1 2026 call]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: Scale + advanced-packaging leadership: the #2 OSAT overall and the leading INDEPENDENT advanced-packaging provider, with HDFO/2.5D platforms qualified at a broadening customer base (5+ on HDFO; half-a-dozen-plus on 2.5D). [Q1 2026 call]

Customer trust + partnership model: deep ties with foundries, fabless leaders, IDMs and OEMs, with customers CO-FUNDING capacity (prepayments/capital support) — de-risking Amkor's investment and locking in demand. [Q1 2026 call]
Geographic footprint incl. the U.S.: the Arizona campus (CHIPS-funded, near TSMC Arizona) positions Amkor as the leading U.S. advanced-packaging partner as supply chains regionalize. [Q1 2026 call]
Second-source value: with foundry in-house packaging (CoWoS) scarce, Amkor is the natural outsourced alternative — customers are 'very motivated' to qualify it quickly. [Q1 2026 call]
facts: Q1 2026: record Q1 revenue $1.68B (+27% YoY), EPS $0.33, gross margin 14.2%, operating margin 6% (+360bps YoY); utilization low-70s% (vs 50s a year earlier). [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-27]
Advanced AI-packaging revenue guided to TRIPLE in 2026; computing end market guided ~+20% for the full year. [Q1 2026 call]
Arizona: ~$7B two-phase campus; $400M CHIPS grant + 35% ITC (~$2.8B support); production 2028, full impact by 2030; ~$1B revenue run-rate potential (>10% of 2025 revenue). [Q1 2026 call]

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Two engines are running: a near-term cyclical recovery (communications/Apple strength, auto advanced, rising utilization) and a structural AI advanced-packaging ramp (computing +20%, AI packaging tripling, the new data-center CPU). The mix-shift toward advanced packaging plus higher utilization is lifting margins off a low base. The catch is that revenue can be 'nonlinear' quarter-to-quarter because customer material (advanced silicon/memory/substrates) sometimes slips, pushing demand around.

competitors.landscape_summary: Packaging/test is split between independent OSATs and the foundries/IDMs that do packaging in-house. Among OSATs, ASE is #1 and Amkor #2, with several Chinese players (JCET, TongFu) and Taiwan's Powertech in the field. Separately, the big foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) do their own advanced packaging — so Amkor both competes with and complements them, increasingly winning OUTSOURCED advanced work as foundry capacity is constrained.

competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: Amkor's edge is being the leading INDEPENDENT advanced-packaging provider — the natural outsourced second source when foundry packaging is full — plus a U.S. footprint (Arizona) that ASE and Chinese rivals lack at the leading edge. Its risks: ASE is bigger; the foundries could keep more advanced packaging in-house; and Chinese OSATs compete hard on price in mainstream.

financial_performance.analyst_view: Amkor is inflecting: +27% Q1 revenue, gross margin and operating margin both expanding off a low base, utilization rising from the 50s to the low-70s, and an AI advanced-packaging ramp guided to triple. The balance sheet (1.1x debt/EBITDA, $2.9B liquidity) comfortably funds the build. Two honest caveats: (1) OSAT margins are structurally thin (gross ~14-15%), so this is a volume/operating-leverage story, not a high-margin one; and (2) Arizona will be a near-term (2027) margin drag before it pays off later in the decade.

valuation.analyst_view: Valuation is the hardest part of the AMKR story. The operational inflection is real (AI packaging tripling, margins expanding, Arizona optionality), but the stock has re-rated ~4x in a year to ~48x trailing earnings for a structurally thin-margin OSAT — and it now trades ABOVE the average analyst target. That combination means the price already embeds a lot of the AI-packaging growth; disappointment on the AI ramp, Arizona timing, or memory/material supply could de-rate it (the 52-week low was $19.79). The May 21 Investor Day's long-range targets are the key catalyst for whether the multiple is justified.

risks.why_it_matters: At ~48x trailing / ~38x forward earnings for a thin-margin OSAT — and trading ABOVE the average analyst target — the stock prices in years of AI-packaging growth; disappointment could de-rate it hard (52-week low $19.79).
A large share of revenue depends on premium-smartphone (iOS) packaging; a shift in that customer's volumes, supply-chain choices, or share would be material.
The 'tripling' depends on advanced-silicon, substrate, and memory supply plus Amkor's own equipment ramp; material slips already cause ~$50-100M/quarter of 'nonlinear' pushouts.
A ~$7B build that dilutes operating margin ~1-2% in 2027 before paying off later; delays, qualification slips, or weak loading would hurt returns.
Gross margins ~14-15% leave little cushion; the model needs high utilization and mix-shift to work, and downturns hit operating leverage in reverse.
Packaging volumes track the broader chip cycle; an AI-capex pause or consumer-demand slump would cut utilization and margins.
ASE is larger; Chinese OSATs press on price; and foundries (TSMC/Samsung/Intel) could keep more advanced packaging in-house, shrinking the outsourced pool.
Middle East-driven commodity/precious-metal and gas costs pressure margins; tariffs and export controls add demand/supply uncertainty.
Sustained $2.5-3.0B CapEx on ~$7B revenue consumes cash and raises execution risk if demand softens after the spend.
The Kim family's majority control limits outside-shareholder influence over strategy and capital allocation.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Amkor Technology (AMKR) is the world's #2 outsourced semiconductor assembly-and-test company (OSAT) and the leading INDEPENDENT provider of advanced packaging — the back-end step that turns a foundry's silicon into a finished, tested chip, and increasingly stitches AI processors together with HBM memory. It sits in the packaging tier of the AI supply chain (one step after TSMC) and is a natural 'second source' as in-house foundry packaging (CoWoS) stays scarce. The business is inflecting: Q1 2026 (reported 2026-04-27) delivered record Q1 revenue of $1.68B (+27% YoY) with EPS of $0.33 (a ~40% beat), gross margin 14.2%, operating margin up 360bps to 6%, and utilization rising from the 50s to the low-70s — and management guides advanced AI-packaging revenue to TRIPLE in 2026, with computing up ~20%. It is also building a ~$7B U.S. advanced-packaging campus in Arizona (with ~$2.8B of CHIPS-grant + tax-credit support) that should scale to full impact by 2030. The balance sheet is healthy (1.1x debt/EBITDA, $2.9B liquidity). The catch is valuation: the stock has re-rated ~4x in a year to ~$83 (an all-time high) and ~$20.5B market cap, trading at ~48x trailing / ~38x forward earnings for a structurally thin-margin OSAT (gross margin ~14-15%) — and it now sits ABOVE the average analyst price target of $75.50. So what is FACT is a genuine AI-packaging-led inflection with expanding margins and a funded U.S. growth project; what is being PRICED is years of that growth compounding flawlessly. The key debates are the AI ramp's durability/linearity and the rich multiple — not whether Amkor is well-positioned in advanced packaging. Watch the May 21 Investor Day for the long-range targets that must justify the valuation.
